citations.F1: N+1: one `users` query per event, up to 1000 sequential round trips per request; fetch all actors in one `WHERE id = ANY($1)` query or JOIN in the main SELECT.
citations.F2: Dedupe is O(n²) (`seen` is a list) and `limit` is applied in Python after fetching every row in the window; ... make `seen` a set if any Python dedupe remains.
citations.F3: `lookup_geo` calls sync `requests.get` (2 s timeout) inside the async handler, once per uncached IP, blocking the event loop for the whole worker; switch to an async client or `run_in_threadpool`
citations.F4: there is no index on `(org_id, created_at)`, so every call sequential-scans 4.2M rows ... `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY events_org_id_created_at_idx ON events (org_id, created_at DESC)`
citations.F5: `_request_timings` appends a float for every request forever (120 req/s × 20 h ≈ 8.6M entries per worker × 4 workers) ... replace with `collections.deque(maxlen=N)` or a real histogram
citations.F6: `_geo_cache` grows unbounded per IP; ... and a TTL/LRU cache for geo
citations.F9: Do not ship the on-call proposal: 16 workers × 50 connections × 6 pods is 4,800 Postgres connections, and more workers multiplies the per-worker memory leak so pods OOM sooner; the Redis cache never hits
citations.F11: the Redis cache never hits because `since` defaults to `now() - 30d` with microsecond precision and the mobile client omits it, so every key is unique
